newsitem.title: PERU: Rebels fire warning shots at Peru hostage site.
newsitem.headline: Rebels fire warning shots at Peru hostage site.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 73 VIP hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima fired several warning shots early on Wednesday after a day of heightened police activity at the site, police said.
At least five shots were heard coming from the rear of the diplomatic compound at about 1 a.m. EST (0600 GMT), police on guard near the residence said.
"They're warning us not to get too close," a police officer about a block from the residence told Reuters.

The shots were immediately followed by silence and there was no movement inside the compound. Police surrounding the residence moved into a state of alert, weapons at the ready, but did not approach, witnesses said.

In a clear signal to the rebels that Tokyo and Lima were united on how to handle the crisis, Japan's Lower House of parliament adopted a resolution denouncing the guerrillas for "conducting criminal acts against the international community."

"We confirm the basic principle of not giving in to terrorism and urge the government to work toward a peaceful resolution of the crisis with the top priority on the lives of the hostages," the resolution approved unanimously by the 500- seat Lower House said.
The shots occured just as police surrounding the compound were changing shifts and followed a day of unusual movements by security forces on Tuesday.

Police had moved to within a few yards (meters) of the front of the property, often running past and peeking through the open gates of the compound. Some policemen threw rocks into the driveway. The purpose of this was unclear.

Police said the detonations sounded like shots from an AKM assault rifle. The roughly 15 jungle-trained Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels are known to possess AKM rifles and grenades and have booby-trapped and mined the compound against possible attack.

The MRTA rebels inside the diplomatic mansion have fired what were later described by police as warning shots several times during the 36-day siege. The previous incidents caused alarm but no injuries, authorities said.
The police movements and shots came as talks to end the five-week-old crisis remained on hold.
Red Cross officials brought in 30 mattresses for the hostages and inspected nearby houses in an apparent bid to find a suitable location for proposed talks.
But the government and the MRTA remained far apart, with the rebels demanding that negotiations include their main demand of freedom for some 400 jailed comrades, and the government rejecting it.
The MRTA rebels initially took about 500 hostages after storming a lavish cocktail party at the residence but have released most in what they called "goodwill gestures."
The remaining 73 include two Peruvian ministers, generals, security chiefs, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats and the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors.

Despite lack of progress to end the crisis, President Alberto Fujimori, whose younger brother Pedro is also held captive, received a boost on Tuesday with pollsters showing most Peruvians approved of his handling of the crisis.

Of 900 Peruvians questioned in the latest survey by Apoyo, a respected polling group, 59 percent thought Fujimori was doing a good job while 30 percent disapproved. The poll also showed Fujimori's popularity crept up two points since December to 47 percent.
The drawn-out hostage crisis appeared to have had the exact opposite effect for Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, according to a poll published in a mayor Tokyo newspaper on Wednesday.

The Yomiuri Shimbum poll of 3,000 people showed approval for Hashimoto's government slipped 4.7 points to 51.8 percent over the last month. The paper said the crisis in Lima had contributed to the drop in support.
Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, has built much of his popularity on an aggressive offensive against the MRTA and the larger and bloodier Maoist Shining Path guerrillas.

A column of about 150 Shining Path rebels on Tuesday set fire to two vehicles on a jungle highway and took a soldier hostage, whom they later released near Tingo Maria about 350 miles (550 km) northeast of Lima, according to the DINCOTE antiterrorist police.

The guerrillas -- known to have entered several towns in central Peru on Monday -- are believed to be carrying out a propaganda offensive in the area to deliver their Maoist message to villagers, according to the DINCOTE.
